Customer support ticket volume jumped 30%. Now what?

The increase tells you what happened, but it doesn't explain why. Before assuming the team is struggling or customers are having more problems, look at which tickets increased and when the change began.

My Customer Support Performance Power BI Kit provides a starting point for exploring these patterns: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4593960875/power-bi-customer-support-dashboard

When ticket volume increases, resist the urge to explain it immediately.

Start by finding where the increase happened. Was it concentrated in billing, technical support, account questions, or a particular channel? A spike in one category tells a very different story from a broad increase across everything.

Try comparing ticket counts by category for the current and previous periods. Look for which categories contributed most to the change before deciding what to investigate.

A ticket volume spike becomes more interesting when you can see exactly when it started.

Did demand climb gradually over several weeks, jump overnight, or appear only during certain hours? Each pattern suggests different questions about customer behavior, product changes, and staffing needs.

My Customer Support Performance Power BI Kit helps you explore ticket trends alongside other service metrics: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4593960875/power-bi-customer-support-dashboard

More support tickets don't automatically mean worse service.

The important question is whether the team can absorb the additional demand. If response times rise, resolution slows, or SLA performance falls, the spike may be creating operational pressure.

Try comparing those three measures before and during your next volume increase. You'll get a clearer picture of whether the extra workload is affecting service delivery.

A support team can handle more tickets without customers having a worse experience.

After checking volume, response times, resolution, and SLA performance, bring customer satisfaction into the picture. If CSAT remains steady despite higher demand, that may be a sign the team is adapting well.

My Customer Support Performance Power BI Kit brings these measures together: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4593960875/power-bi-customer-support-dashboard

A useful support dashboard should help you move beyond reporting that ticket volume increased.

Find where the increase happened, examine when it started, check whether service performance changed, and look for any impact on customer satisfaction. That sequence turns a headline number into a more useful investigation.

If your team's ticket volume suddenly increased 30%, what's the first breakdown or metric you'd want to examine?
